title: The 7 young Wall Street dealmakers helping bankroll the AI infrastructure boom
byline: Alex Nicoll, Alice Tecotzky, Ashley Stewart, Michelle Abrego
excerpt: The AI infrastructure boom is getting more complicated. Meet 7 young Wall Street bankers and investors finding new ways to finance the massive buildout.

By Alex Nicoll

The amount of money needed to fund the future of AI is so large that Wall Street has been rewriting the rules to finance it.

Technology giants have set aside hundreds of billions for the buildout. They've also been running to the debt markets to raise money for their plans. By early August, nearly $500 billion in AI-related debt had been issued in 2026, according to estimates by Goldman Sachs Research.

Financing that buildout is no simple task. It's pushed bankers and investors to develop new financing structures and tap different pools of capital.

The outlook has become more complicated following Democrats' landslide victory in the midterm elections, as many candidates' campaign promises included slowing data center construction and tightening oversight. That scrutiny could potentially delay projects, drive up costs, and make it harder for investors to earn the returns they anticipated.

For Diana Liu, a principal at Blue Owl who has spent more than a decade investing in data centers, navigating these challenges is part of the business.

"Development has never been simple," she told Business Insider following the election. "Experience and long-term local relationships matter more than ever, because a data center project only works when the community, the tenant and the developer all want it to."

Still, the enormous scale of the AI buildout means there will be plenty of work to do.

Meet the crew bankrolling the technology through multibillion-dollar bond offerings, innovative financing, and investments in the power plants and data centers that will underpin the AI economy.

Cody Kiechle, 33, Bank of America

Cody Kiechle is at the center of an unprecedented borrowing spree as technology giants race to build AI infrastructure. Historically, these companies used relatively little outside financing. But Kiechle recognized a turning point in late 2025, when it became clear that their businesses were becoming far more capital-intensive and would turn to debt.

"There was a pretty massive shift happening," he said.

So far in 2026, nine bond offerings have reached $25 billion or more, compared with a previous full-year record of just two deals that size.

Kiechle has led and advised on four of these megadeals. He expects the AI borrowing boom to accelerate into 2027 and believes this period will be remembered as a "seminal moment."

Kiechle's recent deals include helping Alphabet raise $32 billion from investors, securing $25 billion apiece for Oracle and Salesforce, and leading SpaceX's first public bond sale, which raised $25 billion. The Oracle deal attracted a record amount of investor orders for a bond offering from a highly rated company, Kiechle said.

The complexity of these megadeals can be "stressful at times, super exciting at times," Kiechle said. The Alphabet transaction happened over a couple of days, and he worked across multiple time zones to raise money in US dollars, British pounds, and Swiss francs.

Diana Liu, 33, Blue Owl Capital

When Diana Liu worked on her first hyperscale data-center deal in 2016, she had to ask her boss what the term meant. The answer was simple: a really big data center.

But what's considered big has changed dramatically. Back then, a lease for one or two megawatts of computing capacity qualified as hyperscale. Today, the biggest deals are measured in gigawatts — thousands of megawatts.

In her current role as a Principal at Blue Owl, Liu helped develop the novel JV structure behind the financing for Meta's $50 billion Hyperion data center in Louisiana, dubbed Project Beignet.

The deal, financed 80% by Blue Owl and 20% by Meta, raised more than $27 billion and pioneered the use of 144A bonds in data-center financing at an unprecedented scale. The approach gave them access to a wider pool of institutional investors without requiring them to register the securities.

While some may have criticized the deal for taking some of Meta's AI computing costs off its balance sheet, she said it is "the most public deal ever done in data centers" because of the novel use of public bonds.

"It's always been a progression of trying to become a mainstream asset class and be recognized and be able to access traditional forms of markets," Liu said. "This was a push towards that, not trying to hide something."

Maya Venkatraman, 34, Morgan Stanley

Maya Venkatraman played a leading role in structuring a novel $3.2 billion bond for data center developer TeraWulf, with credit support from Google.

"There wasn't really a playbook that existed," said Venkatraman, Morgan Stanley's US head of transportation and infrastructure leveraged finance. Traditional project financing couldn't meet the industry's enormous capital needs alone, so her team developed the structure last fall, which has since served as a template for a market she said has generated roughly $45 billion in high-yield bond issuance over the past year.

Venkatraman also had to educate investors and ratings agencies about the emerging asset class, swapping traditional roadshows for visits to data-center project sites, steel-toed boots and all.

While she knew she had to build something scalable and replicable, she said no one "envisioned the volume of transactions that were gonna follow."

While she's optimistic about AI's long-term potential, Venkatraman is watching whether power availability, construction capacity, and financing can expand together to support the build-out.

"The challenge is really making sure that you can scale all of those things in a coordinated and sustainable way," she said.

For now, debt markets are firing on all cylinders, with new financing structures attracting different pools of investors. But as the AI build-out grows, she said that funding could become the next major constraint. "I think the next sort of constraint to be thoughtful about is capital."

Fiona Ismail, 34, JPMorgan

Fiona Ismail, JPMorgan's global head of investment-grade private credit, has been all in on AI's tremendous capital needs this year.

Throughout the past 12 months, Ismail has spearheaded multiple new types of financings for data center and AI buildouts, including the first 144A financing for a fully completed data center, backed by QTS and Blackstone — a structure that allows companies to raise money from large institutional investors without the traditional securities registration process.

Her team worked with QTS and Blackstone for months, considering many different markets, until Ismail realized that the investment-grade public bond market was the best fit. The transaction eventually "unlocked the public markets for QTS," she said.

"With these financings, you do need a little bit of imagination, and that's one of the things that not having a typical background helps with," Ismail said. "You obviously have to back that up with knowledge of the sector and the industry."

Kate Casey, 32, KKR

Kate Casey is a director in KKR's infrastructure group, helping lead large energy deals that will power hyperscale data centers. The assets her team manages have grown to $119 billion from less than $10 billion when she joined.

This summer, she helped lead KKR's participation in a $5.3 billion investment into a joint venture with energy company Williams to develop natural-gas electricity projects for data centers and other high-energy users.

She works closely with the firm's digital infrastructure team to accelerate data center development, because "increasingly, the ability to deliver that power quickly is what determines how fast a project can move forward."

"I jokingly call our team the data center support team," she said.

Kevin Curtin, 35, JPMorgan

Kevin Curtin is JPMorgan's head of AI infrastructure investment banking, making him the firm's point person in one of the hottest sectors.

His first deal in 2013 was pitching a merger of data center companies DuPont Fabros and Digital Realty. By 2017, the companies had merged, and Curtin had found a rhythm with his teammates. A managing director advised him to branch out, but he doubled down after Microsoft inked a lease for a 400-megawatt data center in 2021.

"I knew that that was going to be a $4 billion construction project and a $5 billion or $6 billion asset. That is bigger than the companies most investment bankers go their entire careers without selling," Curtin said.

Curtin has since broadened JPMorgan's financing toolkit for large-scale digital infrastructure builds by tapping new sources. His team helped data center developer Hut 8 raise $3.25 billion through a 144A bond offering, allowing it to tap major institutional investors to fund construction. He also worked on a first-of-its-kind $1 billion financing for AI-cloud computing company Lambda, backed by contracts with multiple customers, and helped arrange the largest unrated loan ever for AI chip financing: a $5 billion deal for Volta.

Data center financing requires capital from nearly every market, so Curtin is constantly talking with colleagues on other teams.

Jake Epstein, 28, Blackstone

Jake Epstein started his career at Blackstone working on deals across asset classes before Mike Forman, now the digital infrastructure real estate head, recruited him to help the business shortly after Blackstone's purchase of QTS, its US data center platform.

It's been a whirlwind ever since, with Epstein playing a key role in the firm's $7 billion joint venture with Digital Realty in the US in 2023, and on its $16 billion acquisition of Australia-based data-center provider AirTrunk, the following year, alongside his colleagues in Singapore and Sydney.

He now leads a team overseeing major data-center deals, from due diligence and financial analysis to presentations to Blackstone's investment committee. He's also led negotiations on billion-dollar development contracts and leases.

This year, Epstein joined his team to ring the New York Stock Exchange bell for Blackstone's Digital Infrastructure Trust's IPO, which raised $2 billion in the largest-ever blind-pool REIT offering. He was instrumental in developing its novel strategy to acquire stabilized data centers.

As far as AI's impact on the world, he's most excited about potential scientific advances, citing a recent Blackstone paper about AI making phase one clinical trials faster and more successful.

"We're investing in this space to help create new technological and scientific breakthroughs, not just to create AI-generated videos," he said.

2026-11-16T10:52:01.302Z

The amount of money needed to fund the future of AI is so large that Wall Street has been rewriting the rules to finance it.

Technology giants have set aside hundreds of billions for the buildout. They've also been running to the debt markets to raise money for their plans. By early August, nearly $500 billion in AI-related debt had been issued in 2026, according to estimates by Goldman Sachs Research.

Financing that buildout is no simple task. It's pushed bankers and investors to develop new financing structures and tap different pools of capital.

The outlook has become more complicated following Democrats' landslide victory in the midterm elections, as many candidates' campaign promises included slowing data center construction and tightening oversight. That scrutiny could potentially delay projects, drive up costs, and make it harder for investors to earn the returns they anticipated.

For Diana Liu, a principal at Blue Owl who has spent more than a decade investing in data centers, navigating these challenges is part of the business.

"Development has never been simple," she told Business Insider following the election. "Experience and long-term local relationships matter more than ever, because a data center project only works when the community, the tenant and the developer all want it to."

Still, the enormous scale of the AI buildout means there will be plenty of work to do.

Meet the crew bankrolling the technology through multibillion-dollar bond offerings, innovative financing, and investments in the power plants and data centers that will underpin the AI economy.

Cody Kiechle, 33, Bank of America

Cody Kiechle is at the center of an unprecedented borrowing spree as technology giants race to build AI infrastructure. Historically, these companies used relatively little outside financing. But Kiechle recognized a turning point in late 2025, when it became clear that their businesses were becoming far more capital-intensive and would turn to debt.

"There was a pretty massive shift happening," he said.

So far in 2026, nine bond offerings have reached $25 billion or more, compared with a previous full-year record of just two deals that size.

Kiechle has led and advised on four of these megadeals. He expects the AI borrowing boom to accelerate into 2027 and believes this period will be remembered as a "seminal moment."

Kiechle's recent deals include helping Alphabet raise $32 billion from investors, securing $25 billion apiece for Oracle and Salesforce, and leading SpaceX's first public bond sale, which raised $25 billion. The Oracle deal attracted a record amount of investor orders for a bond offering from a highly rated company, Kiechle said.

The complexity of these megadeals can be "stressful at times, super exciting at times," Kiechle said. The Alphabet transaction happened over a couple of days, and he worked across multiple time zones to raise money in US dollars, British pounds, and Swiss francs.

Diana Liu, 33, Blue Owl Capital

When Diana Liu worked on her first hyperscale data-center deal in 2016, she had to ask her boss what the term meant. The answer was simple: a really big data center.

But what's considered big has changed dramatically. Back then, a lease for one or two megawatts of computing capacity qualified as hyperscale. Today, the biggest deals are measured in gigawatts — thousands of megawatts.

In her current role as a Principal at Blue Owl, Liu helped develop the novel JV structure behind the financing for Meta's $50 billion Hyperion data center in Louisiana, dubbed Project Beignet.

The deal, financed 80% by Blue Owl and 20% by Meta, raised more than $27 billion and pioneered the use of 144A bonds in data-center financing at an unprecedented scale. The approach gave them access to a wider pool of institutional investors without requiring them to register the securities.

While some may have criticized the deal for taking some of Meta's AI computing costs off its balance sheet, she said it is "the most public deal ever done in data centers" because of the novel use of public bonds.

"It's always been a progression of trying to become a mainstream asset class and be recognized and be able to access traditional forms of markets," Liu said. "This was a push towards that, not trying to hide something."

Maya Venkatraman, 34, Morgan Stanley

Maya Venkatraman played a leading role in structuring a novel $3.2 billion bond for data center developer TeraWulf, with credit support from Google.

"There wasn't really a playbook that existed," said Venkatraman, Morgan Stanley's US head of transportation and infrastructure leveraged finance. Traditional project financing couldn't meet the industry's enormous capital needs alone, so her team developed the structure last fall, which has since served as a template for a market she said has generated roughly $45 billion in high-yield bond issuance over the past year.

Venkatraman also had to educate investors and ratings agencies about the emerging asset class, swapping traditional roadshows for visits to data-center project sites, steel-toed boots and all.

While she knew she had to build something scalable and replicable, she said no one "envisioned the volume of transactions that were gonna follow."

While she's optimistic about AI's long-term potential, Venkatraman is watching whether power availability, construction capacity, and financing can expand together to support the build-out.

"The challenge is really making sure that you can scale all of those things in a coordinated and sustainable way," she said.

For now, debt markets are firing on all cylinders, with new financing structures attracting different pools of investors. But as the AI build-out grows, she said that funding could become the next major constraint. "I think the next sort of constraint to be thoughtful about is capital."

Fiona Ismail, 34, JPMorgan

Fiona Ismail, JPMorgan's global head of investment-grade private credit, has been all in on AI's tremendous capital needs this year.

Throughout the past 12 months, Ismail has spearheaded multiple new types of financings for data center and AI buildouts, including the first 144A financing for a fully completed data center, backed by QTS and Blackstone — a structure that allows companies to raise money from large institutional investors without the traditional securities registration process.

Her team worked with QTS and Blackstone for months, considering many different markets, until Ismail realized that the investment-grade public bond market was the best fit. The transaction eventually "unlocked the public markets for QTS," she said.

"With these financings, you do need a little bit of imagination, and that's one of the things that not having a typical background helps with," Ismail said. "You obviously have to back that up with knowledge of the sector and the industry."

Kate Casey, 32, KKR

Kate Casey is a director in KKR's infrastructure group, helping lead large energy deals that will power hyperscale data centers. The assets her team manages have grown to $119 billion from less than $10 billion when she joined.

This summer, she helped lead KKR's participation in a $5.3 billion investment into a joint venture with energy company Williams to develop natural-gas electricity projects for data centers and other high-energy users.

She works closely with the firm's digital infrastructure team to accelerate data center development, because "increasingly, the ability to deliver that power quickly is what determines how fast a project can move forward."

"I jokingly call our team the data center support team," she said.

Kevin Curtin, 35, JPMorgan

Kevin Curtin is JPMorgan's head of AI infrastructure investment banking, making him the firm's point person in one of the hottest sectors.

His first deal in 2013 was pitching a merger of data center companies DuPont Fabros and Digital Realty. By 2017, the companies had merged, and Curtin had found a rhythm with his teammates. A managing director advised him to branch out, but he doubled down after Microsoft inked a lease for a 400-megawatt data center in 2021.

"I knew that that was going to be a $4 billion construction project and a $5 billion or $6 billion asset. That is bigger than the companies most investment bankers go their entire careers without selling," Curtin said.

Curtin has since broadened JPMorgan's financing toolkit for large-scale digital infrastructure builds by tapping new sources. His team helped data center developer Hut 8 raise $3.25 billion through a 144A bond offering, allowing it to tap major institutional investors to fund construction. He also worked on a first-of-its-kind $1 billion financing for AI-cloud computing company Lambda, backed by contracts with multiple customers, and helped arrange the largest unrated loan ever for AI chip financing: a $5 billion deal for Volta.

Data center financing requires capital from nearly every market, so Curtin is constantly talking with colleagues on other teams.

Jake Epstein, 28, Blackstone

Jake Epstein started his career at Blackstone working on deals across asset classes before Mike Forman, now the digital infrastructure real estate head, recruited him to help the business shortly after Blackstone's purchase of QTS, its US data center platform.

It's been a whirlwind ever since, with Epstein playing a key role in the firm's $7 billion joint venture with Digital Realty in the US in 2023, and on its $16 billion acquisition of Australia-based data-center provider AirTrunk, the following year, alongside his colleagues in Singapore and Sydney.

He now leads a team overseeing major data-center deals, from due diligence and financial analysis to presentations to Blackstone's investment committee. He's also led negotiations on billion-dollar development contracts and leases.

This year, Epstein joined his team to ring the New York Stock Exchange bell for Blackstone's Digital Infrastructure Trust's IPO, which raised $2 billion in the largest-ever blind-pool REIT offering. He was instrumental in developing its novel strategy to acquire stabilized data centers.

As far as AI's impact on the world, he's most excited about potential scientific advances, citing a recent Blackstone paper about AI making phase one clinical trials faster and more successful.

"We're investing in this space to help create new technological and scientific breakthroughs, not just to create AI-generated videos," he said.
